name: Social Media Branding for Athletes
objectives: Given your sport, values and interests, write a one-sentence brand statement, naming your sport and position, a value and one true thing beyond sport

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What an athlete brand is
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Write a one-sentence brand statement.
This lesson builds toward: Given your sport, values and interests, you will write a one-sentence brand statement, naming your sport and position, a value and one true thing beyond sport.
A brand is the picture people have in their heads when they hear your name. You already have one, whether you planned it or not. Coaches, brands and fans form it from your posts, comments and how you act.
Your brand is more than your sport. It is your sport plus your values plus what makes you you: "A hard-working point guard who loves teaching younger kids and wants to study nursing."
Write a brand statement: "I am a [sport and position] who [what you value or do] and [something else true about you]." Use an AI assistant to suggest wording, but pick words that are honest.
Step by step:
- List your sport and position.
- List three values (like hard work, faith, family, leadership).
- List one interest outside sport.
- Write one brand statement sentence.
Words to know:
- Brand: the picture people have in mind when they hear your name.
- Values: the things that matter most to you and guide how you act.
Try it now: Write your brand statement. Ask an AI assistant for three other ways to word it, then choose or mix the one that sounds most like you.
You can now describe your athlete brand in one honest sentence.

check.q: Do you have a brand if you never planned one?
options: Yes, people form it from your posts, comments and actions
Only if a company sponsors you
check.why: You already have a brand, whether you planned it or not.

check.q: AI suggests a brand statement calling you "the best shooter in the state", which is not true. What do you do?
options: Change it to honest words about you
Post it and see who notices
Ask AI to make it even bigger

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Profile photo, name and bio
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a clear bio and choose a profile photo that match your brand.
This lesson builds toward: On one social media profile, you will write a short bio and choose a profile photo that match your brand, with sport, position, one value and one link, a clear well-lit photo, and no private details.
Your profile is your front door. In a few seconds, people should know who you are, what you play, and why to follow you.
Use a clear, well-lit photo of your face or you in action. Use a name people can find. A strong bio is short: sport and position, level or team (if allowed), one value or interest, and one link or call to action, like your highlight video.
Do not put your home address, phone number, class schedule or exact school location in your bio. If you are a minor, ask a parent or guardian before listing your school or city.
Step by step:
- Choose a clear, well-lit photo.
- Use a findable name.
- Write sport, position and level.
- Add one value or interest.
- Add one link or call to action.
- Remove private details.
Words to know:
- Bio: the short description at the top of your profile.
- Handle: your @username on a social app.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant for five bio options using your brand statement, under the platform's character limit. Pick one, edit it, and update your profile.
You can now write a clear bio and choose a profile photo that match your brand.

check.q: What should people learn from your profile in a few seconds?
options: Who you are, what you play and why to follow you
Every team you ever played for
check.why: Your profile is your front door and should make those three things clear.

check.q: You are 15 and want to add your city and school to your bio. What do you do?
options: Ask a parent or guardian first
check.why: Minors should ask a parent or guardian before listing school or city.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Choosing your content pillars
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Pick three content pillars and two post ideas for each.
This lesson builds toward: Using your brand statement and an AI assistant, you will choose three content pillars with two post ideas for each, with every pillar and idea fitting your brand statement.
Content pillars are the three or four main topics you post about. They keep your feed focused, so people know what to expect.
Athlete pillars might be: Training (workouts, practice clips), Game day (highlights, team moments), Off the field (school, faith, family, hobbies, community service), and Lessons (what you are learning). Pick the ones that match your brand statement.
An AI assistant is good at brainstorming post ideas for each pillar. Ask for ten, then keep the ones you would actually post.
Step by step:
- Read your brand statement.
- Pick three pillars that fit it.
- Ask AI for ten ideas per pillar.
- Keep two you will actually post for each.
Words to know:
- Content pillar: one of the few main topics you regularly post about.
- Feed: the stream of posts on your profile.
Try it now: Write your three content pillars. Use an AI assistant to brainstorm ideas and keep two real post ideas for each pillar.
You can now choose content pillars that match your brand and plan posts for them.

options: To post as often as possible
To keep your feed focused so people know what to expect
check.why: Pillars keep your feed focused on a few main topics.

check.q: Your brand statement mentions faith and community service. Which pillar fits best?
options: Off the field: faith and community service
check.why: Pick pillars that match your brand statement.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Auditing your old posts
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Review your past posts and fix anything that hurts your brand.
This lesson builds toward: On your own profile, you will check your last 30 posts, comments, reposts and tags with the coach, sponsor and grandparent test, archiving, hiding, deleting or untagging everything that fails the test.
Coaches, admissions officers, brands and employers often scroll back through old posts. One old joke, mean comment or reposted video can cost an opportunity.
Do an audit: scroll your last 30 posts, comments, reposts and tagged photos. For each, ask: Would I be okay if a coach, a sponsor or my grandparent saw this? Does it fit my brand? If not, archive, hide or delete it, and untag yourself where you can.
Remember that screenshots last forever. The best protection is posting with care from now on: think before you post, especially when angry after a loss.
Step by step:
- Scroll your last 30 posts, comments, reposts and tags.
- Ask the coach, sponsor and grandparent test.
- Archive, hide or delete what fails.
- Untag yourself where needed.
- Make a rule: no posting when angry.
Words to know:
- Audit: a careful check of everything, to find and fix problems.
- Archive: hide a post from your profile without deleting it.
Try it now: Audit your last 30 posts and tagged photos. Write how many you kept, archived and deleted.
You can now audit your social media and remove posts that hurt your brand.

check.q: What should your audit include besides your own posts?
check.why: The audit covers posts, comments, reposts and tags.

check.q: An old repost of a mean video fails the grandparent test. What do you do?
check.why: Archive, hide or delete what fails the test.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Privacy and safety settings
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set your accounts so you control who sees and contacts you.
This lesson builds toward: In each app's settings, you will set who can message, comment and tag you, turn off location on posts and turn on two-step verification, with every setting checked and a plan to save proof, block, report and tell an adult if threatened.
Being public helps you get seen, but it also lets strangers find you. Many athletes keep one public athlete account and one private personal account.
Check your settings on each app: who can message you, who can comment, who can tag you, whether your location is added to posts, and two-step verification to protect your login. Settings menus change, so look for privacy, security and messaging in the app's settings.
Never post your live location, travel plans in real time, home or daily routine. Be careful with direct messages from people you do not know, including fake recruiters and fake brands. If someone threatens you or asks for private photos, do not reply; save proof, block, report, and tell a trusted adult or your coach.
Step by step:
- Decide: public athlete account and private personal account?
- Limit who can message, comment and tag you.
- Turn off location on posts.
- Turn on two-step verification.
- Know how to block and report.
Words to know:
- Two-step verification: a second check, like a code, when you log in, so others cannot get in with just your password.
- Direct message (DM): a private message sent on a social app.
Try it now: Open the settings on one account. Limit who can message and tag you, turn off location on posts, and turn on two-step verification.
You can now set your accounts so you control who sees and contacts you.

check.why: Two-step verification adds a second check to protect your login.

check.q: A stranger who says they are a recruiter keeps messaging and asks for private photos. What do you do?
options: Send a photo to keep them happy
Do not reply; save proof, block, report and tell a trusted adult
check.why: Never reply to threats or requests for private photos; save proof and get help.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Staying on-brand: rules, brands and judgment
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write your personal posting rules, including how to handle sponsored posts.
This lesson builds toward: Using your team's rules, you will write your personal posting rules, including how you disclose brand deals and handle negative comments, with three "I always" rules, three "I never" rules and a disclosure and NIL check rule.
Your team, school or league may have social media rules, especially about team news, injuries, recruiting and rivals. Ask your coach for them and follow them.
As your brand grows, brands may offer free products or money to post. The FTC says you must clearly disclose any paid deal or free product right in the post. College athletes may also have NIL reporting rules, and high school rules vary by state. Ask your compliance office or state athletic association before accepting.
Write a short list of your own posting rules: what you post, what you never post, and how you handle negative comments (do not argue; mute, hide or block).
Step by step:
- Get your team's social media rules from your coach.
- Write three "I always" rules.
- Write three "I never" rules.
- Write how you handle negative comments.
- Add: "I disclose any brand deal and check NIL rules first."
Words to know:
- NIL: name, image and likeness: an athlete earning money from their name, photo or personal brand.
- Disclosure: a clear statement in the post that you were paid or given something.
Official sources:
- FTC: Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers
- NCAA: Name, Image and Likeness
Try it now: Final task: write your posting rules, then finish branding one profile: brand statement, bio and photo, three pillars with two ideas each, a 30-post audit and safe settings.
You can now keep your brand on track with clear posting rules and honest handling of brand deals.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Brand statement Missing, vague, or not honest. One honest sentence with sport and position, a value and one interest beyond sport. The bio, photo and pillars all clearly match the statement. Bio and photo No link or call to action, an unclear photo, or private details showing. A short bio with sport, position, one value and one link, a clear photo, and no private details. The link goes to an up-to-date highlight video or recruiting profile. Content pillars Fewer than three pillars, or ideas that do not fit the brand. Three pillars with two post ideas each that fit the brand statement. Ideas are scheduled across the next two weeks. Post audit Fewer than 30 posts checked, or posts that fail the test are still visible. The last 30 posts, comments, reposts and tags checked, with failing items archived, hidden, deleted or untagged. The audit goes back further and a "no posting when angry" rule is written. Privacy and safety Location still on posts, open messaging, or no two-step verification. Messaging, comments and tags limited, location off and two-step verification on. A separate private personal account is set up and the athlete can show how to block and report. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does the FTC say about a free product you post about?
options: Disclose it clearly right in the post
Put it in your bio once
No disclosure is needed for students
check.why: Any paid deal or free product must be clearly disclosed in the post.

check.q: Someone posts a rude comment after your team loses. What does your rule say?
options: Do not argue; mute, hide or block
check.why: Your posting rules say how to handle negative comments without arguing.
